<reason>Side B won the burden battle from the opening and never lost it. The motion's "only" makes work, appeal, and family unity individually necessary conditions, and B correctly isolated the dispute onto the two contested rights while conceding appeal as floor. B's pressure question about single adults (a reunification right that does no work in most transfers cannot be necessary in all) was never fully neutralized — A's "rules apply blindly" answer was met by B's sharp counter that family ties surface at the claim interview before transfer. B also landed the Canada reductio and then flipped A's own answer (courts make remedies real = enforceable adjudication = B's floor) into evidence for B's frame. A fought well: the substitutes pressure question forced B to produce the debate's best single move — the functional line that appeal protects against error where only review corrects error, while destitution has a genuine substitute in reception support. A's closing dilemma on whether reception support is enforceable or discretionary was clever, but B's closing dispatch showed both horns fail the motion. A's clipped closing and B's clipped rebuttal were minor execution costs on each side. On balance, B's necessity arithmetic ("three promised, one defended") gave the cleaner reason to vote, and B answered more of the live pressure directly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 [B4.1]–[B4.2]: asked why a missing work right can be excused by substitutes but a missing appeal cannot, B drew a genuinely principled functional line — adjudicative error can only be corrected by review, while destitution can be fully secured by reception support — turning A's sharpest pressure question into a structural win. B then compounded it in [B4.6] by showing that A's own Canada analysis was decided by enforceable adjudication alone, with work and family rights as scenery.</best_rebuttal>
